paras: The attempted lynching of R. D. Raven took place at Waverly, Lancaster County, Nebraska, on the night of February 20, 1882, when a crowd seized Raven, who was accused of shooting James Cook dead in a dispute over the spelling of a word, and put a rope over his head. Sheriff Ensign and Deputy Sheriff Mellick got him away from the crowd and took him to the jail at Lincoln on a passing special train. Papers across the country treated it as a curiosity, a killing over spelling that nearly ended in a hanging; none gave the race of anyone involved.

Waverly lay about twelve miles east of Lincoln. Cook was described as a merchant or a grain buyer; the Grant County Herald of Lancaster, Wisconsin, added that he was "quite prominent in local politics" and recently married to Emma Coumbe, formerly of Lancaster. The accused man's name appeared as R. D. Raven, R. B. Raiven, R. P. Raiven and Dick Rayner; he was called a painter and a native of Kentucky, and the Warren Sheaf described him as a "tramp painter" considered "a dangerous character."

According to the Lincoln dispatch of February 21, the two young men disputed the spelling of a word, Raven called Cook "an approbrious epithet," and Cook struck him with his pistol. Other versions said Cook struck him with his fist, or that Cook had been asked to decide the spelling, ruled against Raven, and was called a liar before he hit him. Raven then drew a revolver and shot Cook through the body, or through the heart in other accounts, and Cook died within minutes.

In the Chicago Times account, Raven ran to a nearby stable and mounted a horse that refused to go, and the crowd surrounded and captured him. Amid what the account called intense excitement, the crowd procured a rope and got it around Raven's neck. The Lincoln dispatch said Deputy Sheriff Mellick and the prisoner struggled out of a door, someone cried murder, and Sheriff Ensign came up, dispersed the crowd and secured the prisoner.

A passing Chicago, Burlington and Quincy special train carrying railroad officials was stopped, and the sheriff took Raven aboard to the Lincoln jail. The Herald's account said the prisoner "was terribly frightened" and begged the sheriff to save him from the lynchers.

No arrests of members of the crowd were reported, and no report of an inquest, indictment or trial was found in the coverage. In August 1882 The Frontier of O'Neill City, Nebraska, recalling a murder over spelling at Waverly the previous winter, said that the murderer was "now serving out a life sentence," though it named no one and gave no source.

The story first moved as a Lincoln wire dated February 21, which ran the next day in the Wheeling Register and the Rock Island Argus, and as a one-line item in the Memphis Daily Appeal that put Waverly in Mississippi. A longer account credited to the Chicago Times, headed "A Referee in a Spelling Match Shot Dead" in the Wilmington Daily Republican, added the stable, the telegram to Lincoln and the special train. Weekly papers in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Tennessee and Kansas reprinted condensed versions into early March, usually in crime roundups beside other shootings. One roundup, in a second item, reported Cook murdered at Waverly by "a tramp painter named Dick Rayner."

Headlines stressed the trivial cause, as in the Warren Sheaf's "Murder from a Trivial Cause" and the Wheeling Register's "A Western Killing." Writing for readers who knew Cook's widow, the Grant County Herald called the shooting a "dastardly murder" by a "rascally murderer" and remarked that without the special train Raiven "would have undoubtedly ornamented a telegraph pole before morning." The Arizona Weekly Citizen made a joke of it, writing that "the company prepared to hang Mr. Raiven without delay or shrift."

The Lincoln dispatch of February 21, the closest source, dated the shooting to "last night," February 20, while the Wilmington paper said "Tuesday night," the Arizona Weekly Citizen the 21st, and one roundup item the 19th. Two papers placed the shooting at Lincoln rather than Waverly, and the Warren Sheaf put it in a bar room.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of R. D. Raven
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd seized R. D. Raven, accused of shooting James Cook, and put a rope over his head or around his neck intending to hang him, but officers took him away to the Lincoln jail (A1, A11, A13).

A crowd acting without authority tried to hang Raven for the shooting of Cook, but he was rescued by the sheriff and his deputy and no one was killed by the crowd (A1, A11); this was an attempted lynching.
The Lincoln wire (A1, A2) and the separately written Chicago Times account (A4, A11) agree on the shooting at Waverly, the crowd's rope and the officers' rescue.

accounts.label: Lincoln wire (Feb. 21)
accounts.gist: Raven and Cook disputed a spelling; Raven insulted Cook, Cook struck him with his pistol, Raven shot him; a crowd threw a rope over Raven's head, but the deputy and the sheriff got him away and took him to Lincoln by special train.

accounts.label: Chicago Times account
accounts.gist: Cook, asked to decide a spelling, ruled against Raiven, who called him a liar; Cook struck him and was shot through the heart; Raiven fled to a stable, was captured, and had a rope round his neck before the sheriff and deputy rescued him and boarded a passing special train.

accounts.label: Warren Sheaf version
accounts.gist: In a bar room Cook took sides against Raven in a discussion and struck him after being called a liar; Raven was arrested and taken to Lincoln because a crowd had arranged to hang him at once.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Lincoln wire or condensed versions in crime roundups ('Crimes and Casualties', 'Criminal', 'Tragical Tales') without comment on the crowd.
The Grant County Herald called the shooting a 'dastardly murder' by a 'rascally murderer' and said Raiven would have 'ornamented a telegraph pole' but for the train, without criticizing the crowd.
Headlines stressed the trivial cause: 'Murder from a Trivial Cause', 'A Referee in a Spelling Match Shot Dead'.
The Arizona Weekly Citizen treated the episode as a joke about 'orthographical controversies', including the company's preparation to hang Raiven.
